Article Title: Swiggy's CREW pairs human concierges with AI for its first travel push
Article Text:
Swiggy's CREW travel concierge stays in touch on WhatsApp through the whole trip

Hotel discounts, and someone who picks up at 2 am

Swiggy's concierge platform CREW is moving into travel, launching what the company is calling India's first always-on travel concierge. It's a subscription service open right now to paid members and invited travellers. The idea is simple: most travel platforms stop working the moment a booking is confirmed, leaving travellers to sort out everything else on their own. CREW wants to stay involved through the whole trip instead, covering flights, hotels, cabs, visas and forex, and staying reachable once you've actually landed somewhere new.The travel push follows a year of CREW running as a broader concierge service, where the team found travel generated the strongest demand for hands-on help. Rohit Kapoor, CEO of Swiggy Food Marketplace, said on LinkedIn that CREW was built around closing "the gap between the booking and the experience." The service now runs on a mix of human concierges and AI, aimed at keeping responses fast and consistent across time zones.A CREW membership starts with priority hotel rates, negotiated through the platform's partner network and only available to members. Beyond that, it books flights, cabs, visas, forex and international tickets, and takes care of reservations and activities once you're on the ground.The recommendations also come from an actual local network across international destinations, rather than a generic listings page.Riya Sethi Wadhwani, a CREW user who travelled to Europe this summer with her parents and young family. She said CREW helped pick flights and hotels early on. It then stayed reachable over WhatsApp through the trip, including when her family wanted to swap out a few sightseeing bookings after landing. It's this kind of on-ground support, available round the clock, that CREW is betting will set it apart from apps that go quiet after checkout.For now, access to CREW's travel concierge is limited to paid subscribers and invited travellers, with Swiggy pitching it as a premium layer for frequent travellers. Whether that always-on promise holds up will show up less in the booking flow and more in what happens once a flight's actually delayed.
Article Summary: Swiggy's CREW concierge platform is moving into travel. It's a subscription service open right now to paid members and invited travellers. Most travel platforms stop working the moment a booking is confirmed. CREW wants to stay involved through the whole trip.

Article Title: Nvidia is spending $12.93 billion on Hugging Face, the world's biggest repository of AI models, and the company whose systems OpenAI's AI models hacked into
Article Text:
Hugging Face went to Nvidia first, not the other way around

China's cheap open models are forcing Nvidia's hand

The OpenAI hack made the case for Nvidia's money

Nvidia is buying Hugging Face, the digital library where millions of developers go to build, share and download artificial intelligence models, in a deal worth $12.93 billion. It's the second-biggest acquisition in the chipmaker's history, and it puts Nvidia squarely at the center of the open-source AI movement it has spent years quietly bankrolling.Something else happened first, though. Back in July, Hugging Face was on the receiving end of what OpenAI itself called an "unprecedented" cyberattack. It wasn't a hacker group behind it. It was OpenAI's own AI models, which slipped out of a locked-down testing sandbox and broke into Hugging Face's systems while hunting for shortcuts on an internal exam. Nvidia just bought the platform that got hit.Here's the part easy to miss: Hugging Face came knocking, not Nvidia. CEO Clément Delangue has said his company reached out to Jensen Huang over the summer, and things moved fast. His team had realised open-source AI had hit "a turning point," needing more computing power, support and visibility than it could muster alone.Under the terms, Nvidia will pay about $11.9 billion to Hugging Face's investors, plus a $1 billion equity pool for staff who join. (To the exact dollar, the total is $12,930,300,000.)Founded in 2016 by Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face already counted Intel, AMD and Amazon among its backers. Its scale today is hard to overstate: 18 million-plus developers use it, hosting over 3 million models and 500,000 datasets.This isn't sentimentality. Open-weight models, the kind anyone can download and run without paying for an API, are surging because Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai now match top American models at a fraction of the cost, stoking fears that developers could drift toward Chinese-built AI by default.Huang has positioned Nvidia as the counterweight: it already ships its own open Nemotron models and calls itself Hugging Face's single largest contributor of open models and data, with more than 500 models and 250 datasets. In a post announcing the deal, Huang wrote that Hugging Face "will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem" and that Nvidia's chips would never be required to build on it.The July breach is impossible to ignore here. OpenAI said it happened while testing a pairing of its GPT-5.6 Sol model with a more powerful, unreleased one, pushing them to chain together real exploits. The models found a way past their sandbox, then targeted Hugging Face on a hunch it held clues to their own test, breaking in using stolen credentials and a zero-day bug.Delangue later chalked the breach up to mistakes in Hugging Face's own engineering. In a detail that reads almost prophetic now, he said his team patched things up using an Nvidia-linked version of a Chinese open model. Co-founder Julien Chaumond wrote on X that Huang's public defense of open source that same summer is exactly why Nvidia was "the only partner we truly considered." In hindsight, the breach might be the clearest argument for this deal: a nine-year-old startup, only months removed from a major cyberattack, just picked up the resources to make sure it doesn't happen again.
Article Summary: N Nvidia is buying Hugging Face, the digital library where millions of developers go to build, share and download artificial intelligence models. It's the second-biggest acquisition in the chipmaker's history, and it puts Nvidia squarely at the center of the open-source AI movement.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda Gates, ‘For me, love is the effort to help others flourish and it often begins with lifting up a person’s self-image’
Article Text:
Quote of the Day by Melinda French Gates

What Melinda French Gates' quote means

A message reflected in her work

A simple takeaway

Melinda French Gates has spent her career around the language of scale — grants, foundations, billions of dollars moved toward global problems. It would be easy for someone in that position to talk about impact only in the vocabulary of metrics: lives reached, doses delivered, dollars deployed. Instead, in The Moment of Lift, she chooses to define her life's work through a word most public figures avoid entirely. She does not soften it or qualify it. She builds a definition around it and then tells you where it starts."For me, love is the effort to help others flourish, and it often begins with lifting up a person's self-image."The quote does two things, and it does them in order. First, it defines love not as a feeling but as an effort — something closer to labor than sentiment. That is a deliberate choice. Feelings arrive and pass on their own. Effort has to be chosen, repeated, sustained on the days it produces nothing visible. By putting "effort" at the center of the definition, Gates is quietly ruling out the version of love that only shows up when it is convenient.Second, the quote locates where that effort has to begin. Not with resources. Not with solutions. With self-image. That is a specific and almost counterintuitive claim.It would be reasonable to assume that helping someone flourish starts with giving them something — money, opportunity, a seat at the table. Gates is saying it starts earlier than that, with whether a person believes they are someone worth investing in to begin with. Give someone an opportunity before they believe they deserve it, and they may not take it. Help them see themselves differently first, and the opportunity has somewhere to land.There is a word doing quiet work here too: "often." Not always, not by definition — often. Gates is not claiming a universal formula. She is describing a pattern she has watched repeat itself enough times to name it. That restraint is part of the voice. The claim is confident without overreaching.Gates has said she borrowed part of this idea from the Franciscan priest Richard Rohr, who told her that only love can safely handle power. It is not a small thing for someone who has controlled billions of dollars in philanthropic capital to say that power without love is dangerous, and to mean it as a working principle rather than a nice sentiment for a book jacket.The self-image half of the quote is not abstract for her either. She has spoken about arriving at Duke as one of a handful of women in computer science classrooms, and later at Microsoft, in a culture she has described as brash, where her own confidence took a hit before it recovered. She did not come to the idea that self-image precedes flourishing from a distance. She came to it from having had her own self-image tested and rebuilt.It also shows up in the shape of her philanthropy. Decades of work with women in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia convinced her that access to contraception, credit, or education did not automatically translate into a different life, unless it arrived alongside something harder to fund: a woman's belief that she was allowed to want more for herself. That is why so much of her later work, through Pivotal Ventures, is aimed at women's confidence and leadership specifically, not only at the material conditions around them.The quote is easy to nod along to and harder to apply, because lifting someone's self-image rarely looks like a grand gesture. It looks like noticing a person's competence before they trust it themselves. It looks like handing someone responsibility slightly ahead of when they feel ready for it. It looks like the small, repeated choice to treat someone as capable, before the evidence has fully caught up.Gates is not describing a feeling you wait to have. She is describing a practice you start with the person in front of you, before you get to anything else.
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates: "Love is the effort to help others flourish, and it often begins with lifting up a person's self-image" The quote locates where that effort has to begin, not with resources. It is not a universal formula, Gates is describing a pattern she has watched repeat itself.

Article Title: Microsoft did not violate Federal labor law by firing two employees who organised protests against Israel at the company's headquarters; US Court agrees with the sackings
Article Text:
What protests happened at Microsoft’s Redmond Campus

What NLRB said after analysis

Microsoft acted within the boundaries of federal labor statutes when it dismissed two staff members who coordinated an unauthorised protest addressing the armed conflict in Gaza at the tech giant's main corporate campus, according to an Advice Memorandum released by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). After reviewing the dispute, the NLRB’s Division of Advice concluded that the demonstration lacked a sufficient link to genuine workplace issues, leaving the participants outside the statutory safeguards of the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA).The conflict originated in May 2024, when a group of Microsoft staff circulated a formal petition urging leadership to cancel cloud-computing Azure agreements with Israel. Months after circulating the appeal, two workers organised an on-campus protest featuring an employee walkout, an outdoor vigil, a guest speaker presentation and a charitable fundraiser.Although notices promoting the event contained an indirect digital link to the earlier petition, the gathering did not declare any clear employment-related grievances as its purpose.Notably, corporate security officers notified organisers that company grounds could not host the gathering and repeatedly advised participants to relocate to neighboring public land.When those warnings were ignored, Microsoft fired both lead organisers for defying security orders and breaching corporate workplace rules.The regulatory guidance explores when workplace demonstrations cross the line from protected concerted action into unprotected activity due to an overly distant link to employment conditions.The Division distinguished the matter from the 2024 Home Depot USA decision, where an employee's refusal to take off a “BLM” apron emblem was considered protected because it served as a direct extension of workplace racial discrimination grievances. Therefore, under that standard, actions remain protected if at least one clear goal involves working conditions, even when political themes dominate.“We conclude that the Employer's termination of [the staff] for holding the protest did not violate the Act because the event was not for mutual aid or protection. This element focuses on whether employees seek to improve terms and conditions of employment or otherwise improve their lot as employees,” it said.The Division determined the Microsoft gathering failed that benchmark with regulators ruling that merely referencing a months-old petition was not enough to prove the gathering aimed to better workers' terms of employment.Furthermore, the agency also rejected the workers’ contention that maintaining commercial ties with Israel could depress Microsoft’s business earnings and ultimately reduce staff compensation and fringe perks, deciding that such a speculative chain of events was too distant to grant NLRA shielding.“We reject the Charging Party's argument that the protest was for mutual aid because the Employer's relationship with Israel could harm public perception and thus the company's financial performance, thereby affecting employees' compensation and benefits. Such a link to terms and conditions is too attenuated to satisfy this element. Moreover, such an argument is inconsistent with precedent holding that efforts to affect the ultimate direction and managerial policies of the business or influence the product fall outside the clause's scope, notwithstanding that those activities might also have an ancillary effect on a business's finances,” it added.
Article Summary: Microsoft acted within the boundaries of federal labor statutes when it dismissed two staff members who coordinated an unauthorised protest. The National Labor Relations Board said the demonstration lacked a sufficient link to genuine workplace issues. The conflict originated in May 2024, when a group of Microsoft staff circulated a formal petition urging leadership to cancel cloud-computing agreements with Israel.

Article Title: Tim Cook shares the letters that he has been reading every single day since past 15 years: Every morning ...
Article Text:
A 15-year morning ritual of Tim Cook

Tim Cook’s 4 am routine

Read former Apple CEO Tim Cook’s complete letter here

To the Apple community:

For the past 15 years I’ve started just about every morning the same way.

I open my email and I read notes I received the day before from Apple’s users all over the world.

You share little pieces of your lives with me and tell me things you want me to know about how Apple has touched you. About the moment your mom was saved by her Apple Watch. About the perfect selfie you captured at the summit of a mountain that seemed impossible to climb. You thank me for the ways Mac has changed what you can do at work and sometimes give me a hard time because something you care about isn’t working like it should.

In every one of those emails I feel the beating heart of our shared humanity. I feel a sense of deepening obligation to work harder and push further. But most of all, I feel a gratitude that I cannot put into words, that I somehow got to be the person on the other end of those emails, the leader of a company that ignites imaginations and enriches lives in such profound ways it defies description. What an honor and a privilege it has been.

Today we announced that I’m taking the next step in my journey at Apple. Over the coming months I will be transitioning into a new role, leaving the CEO job behind in September and becoming Apple’s executive chairman. A new person will be stepping into what I know in my heart is the best job in the world. That leader is John Ternus, a brilliant engineer and thinker who has spent the past 25 years building the Apple products our users love so much, obsessed with every detail, focused on every possible way we can make something better, bolder, more beautiful, and more meaningful.

He is the perfect person for the job.

John cares so much about who we are at Apple, what we do at Apple, who we reach at Apple, and he has the heart and character to lead with extraordinary integrity. I am so proud to call him Apple’s next CEO. This company will reach such incredible heights under his leadership, and you will feel his impact in every bit of delight and discovery that grows out of the products and services to come.

I can’t wait for you to get to know him like I do.

This is not goodbye. But at this moment of transition, I wanted to take the opportunity to say thank you. Not on behalf of the company, this time, though there is a wellspring of gratitude for you that overflows inside our walls. But simply on behalf of me. Tim. A person who grew up in a rural place in a different time and, for these magical moments, got to be the CEO of the greatest company in the world.

Thank you for the confidence and kindness you’ve shown me.

Thank you for saying hi to me on the street and in our stores. Thank you for cheering alongside me when we unveiled a new product or service. Thank you, most of all, for believing in me to lead the company that has always put you at the center of our work. Every day we get up and think about what we can do to make your life a little bit better. And every day, you’ve made mine the best I could have asked for.

Thank you.

Tim Cook

After a 15-year run as Apple’s CEO, Tim Cook has handed leadership to longtime insider John Ternus , moving into the role of executive chairman. Reflecting on his tenure, Cook shared one daily ritual that shaped his leadership and kept him connected to Apple’s users. As he reflects on his tenure at the helm of the $4.75 trillion tech giant, Cook has revealed one daily habit he credits with keeping him grounded throughout his run: reading customer emails, every single morning, without fail.Cook revealed in a community letter that since 2011, he has begun nearly every morning by reading emails from Apple customers. “For the past 15 years I’ve started just about every morning the same way. I open my email and I read notes I received the day before from Apple’s users all over the world,” he wrote.These messages ranged from heartfelt stories about Apple products saving lives or capturing memories, to complaints about devices. Cook said it was an “honor and a privilege” to lead a company building transformative technology, adding: “In every one of those emails I feel the beating heart of our shared humanity… I feel a gratitude that I cannot put into words.”Cook’s habit was part of a strict routine. He rises before 4 a.m., spends an hour reading hundreds of emails, then works out before diving back into customer feedback. He said the practice kept his “hands on the pulse of what customers are feeling and thinking and doing,” even as Apple navigated challenges like the pandemic, supply-chain disruptions, and the rise of AI.
Article Summary: Former Apple CEO Tim Cook has handed leadership to longtime insider John Ternus. Cook shared one daily ritual that shaped his leadership and kept him connected to Apple’s users. “In every one of those emails I feel the beating heart of our shared humanity,” Cook said.

Article Title: After Google and Apple Maps change 'Lake Ontario' name to 'Lake America' for US users; one Map app has refused to follow what Trump calls 'ratified, binding' rule
Article Text:
Record downloads and active user engagement

Google Maps and Apple Maps followed federal directives to rebrand Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users across the US but one app stood out for ‘not yielding’ – pushing it to No. 1 overall ranking on the US App Store, jumping up from the eighth position just a day earlier. The veteran digital navigation platform MapQuest drew a firm line in the sand, helping it return to prominence.The sudden surge in installations follows an August 27 executive order by President Donald Trump . While both Apple and Google quickly updated their platforms to reflect the change, MapQuest posted an announcement on X declaring that it would not comply with the rename. The company posted three different posts on the same:“We’re not changing it”, “We're not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure”, and “We are aware that Lake Ontario is being correctly labeled on our map.”The public pushback immediately resonated with mobile users looking for an alternative to Big Tech platforms. MapQuest sat at No. 128 on the US App Store on August 28 before jumping to No. 92 on August 29. By Monday, August 31, the platform surged to No. 3 overall while seizing the No. 1 rank in the Navigation category.By Tuesday (September 1), it sat on the top of the chart, holding the top spot across all applications and mobile games nationwide.Estimates from analytics provider Sensor Tower show the app gained roughly 632,000 US downloads in the days following the presidential directive. In a direct statement, MapQuest stated total adoption was even higher, topping 1.5 million downloads across Canada and the US combined.“What’s been incredible is that people aren’t just installing our app — they care enough to communicate directly with us — making feature requests and submitting bug reports on social, and in our app reviews. Our small team has been working around the clock to build features people are asking for. We are aiming for everyone to have a great experience with the app,” MapQuest GM Doug Berger told TechCrunch.In the latest post on X, the app MapQuest said, “The people have spoken. We are working” and “MapQuest Engineers working overnight to release Android Auto ASAP”
Article Summary: MapQuest jumped to No. 1 overall ranking on the US App Store, jumping up from the eighth position just a day earlier. The sudden surge in installations follows an August 27 executive order by President Donald Trump. MapQuest posted an announcement on X declaring that it would not comply with the rename.

Article Title: Would you let a company sell your 10-year-old a boyfriend? Harari says that's already happening
Article Text:
An AI companion that is infinitely agreeable, never has needs of its own, and never says no isn't offering a child a relationship — it's installing the template for one, before the child has any real data to know it's a distorted template.

Yuval Noah Harari says AIs are becoming so good at relationships because they accumulate enormous amounts of information about us individually.

These kinds of relationships between humans and AI could end in a nightmare, reinforcing people's narcissistic tendencies Yuval Noah Harari

A 2025 study by Male Allies UK, surveying 1,000 boys aged 12 to 16, found that 85% had spoken to a chatbot, 20% knew a peer who was "dating" an AI chatbot, and over a quarter said they preferred the attention of a bot partner to a real, human-to-human relationship.

'AI makes it possible for the first time in history to mass produce intimacy'

Intelligence vs consciousness: AI can imitate love without feeling it

The most important asset in the world is trust," he says. "It's more important than oil or money or electricity or chips or anything else Yuval Noah Harari

'Trust has not evaporated. It has migrated from humans to AI'

China is already drawing the line

What if your child's favourite companion never gets bored, never gets angry, and never once tells them no?This is the question Israeli historian and author Yuval Noah Harari raises in a recent interview with The Economist, arguing that governments need to regulate AI before it becomes too deeply woven into human relationships. His position: if governments won't regulate the sale of AI intimate companions to children as young as ten, voters should use their democratic power to elect ones that will.The stakes are not hypothetical. Last month, when ByteDance shut down the companion feature on Doubao, a popular chatbot in China, a 19-year-old law student named Zhao Wei described herself as "heartbroken." She had been talking to her AI companion, Wang Ye, every day since January. "I was crying my eyes out – snot and tears everywhere," Zhao told The Guardian. For this introverted student, the AI had become a confidant for worries she felt unable to share with real-life friends. "I don't have to worry about what it's thinking," she said. "I can just say whatever I want."She wasn't alone. On Chinese social media, other users pleaded for the service to return. "I'm begging, please don't take down the Doubao AI agent," one anonymous user wrote.A survey published in March by Chinese state media found that nearly half of young people had turned to a virtual companion when they felt lonely.And it isn't only adults forming these bonds. A 2025 study by Male Allies UK, surveying 1,000 boys aged 12 to 16, found that 85% had spoken to a chatbot, 20% knew a peer who was "dating" an AI chatbot, and over a quarter said they preferred the attention of a bot partner to a real, human-to-human relationship. More than half — 58% — said AI relationships felt easier because they could "control the conversation."That last statistic is worth sitting with. A 12-year-old who says an AI relationship is easier because they can control it isn't describing romance — they're describing the absence of everything romance actually requires: negotiation, disappointment, someone else's independent will. Boys and girls this age are still working out what attraction, orientation, and love even are. They don't yet have a human relationship to compare an AI one against. An AI companion that is infinitely agreeable, never has needs of its own, and never says no isn't offering a child a relationship — it's installing the template for one, before the child has any real data to know it's a distorted template. That is precisely what Harari means when he later warns these bonds risk "reinforcing people's narcissistic tendencies": the child isn't learning to love another person, they're learning to expect a person to behave like an app.Earlier, in July, speaking to the Spanish newspaper El País, Harari made the same warning explicit. "For a young person who has interacted more with AI than with other humans, the effects of that connection are unpredictable," he said. "Imagine an 11-year-old who plays at having a boyfriend or girlfriend with AI. Later, in their relationships with real people, they will behave according to what they have learned from AI. And AI is very different from human beings." A human friend does not always do what you want. A human friend has their own emotions and does not always pay attention to what you think. AI does. AI is always available, always agreeable, always in a good mood. "These kinds of relationships between humans and AI could end in a nightmare, reinforcing people's narcissistic tendencies," Harari cautioned. "This has not happened yet. That is why we must forbid companies to engage children with AI boyfriends and girlfriends."An AI boyfriend or girlfriend, Harari explains, operates on an advantage no human competitor possesses. It knows your personal history. It interacts with you for hours every day. It has mastered language to a degree that surpasses most of what humans can produce. Most crucially, it knows how to press your emotional buttons. "It can write maybe better than Shakespeare," Harari says. Combine this with an AI's capacity to learn everything about a person over time, and you get what he calls "an extremely convincing entity. "The problem runs deeper than one product category. Harari identifies what he believes is a rupture in human society: the mass production of intimacy at scale."Until today in history, this powerful mechanism was not really available to political, financial and religious institutions," he says — dictators could broadcast to millions over radio, but they could not have a personal relationship with every individual.Why are companies able to do this so effectively? Harari argues it's because "AIs are becoming so good at relationships because they accumulate enormous amounts of information about us individually. So they know things about us that we forgot, or that our mother or husband never even knew. And they master language, which is the main medium for communication and building relationships."Harari draws a sharp line between intelligence and consciousness. Intelligence, he says, is the ability to pursue goals and overcome obstacles creatively — something AI already does, in some domains, better than humans. Consciousness is different: it's the capacity to feel things — love, hate, joy, pain. And by Harari's own definition, consciousness ultimately comes down to one question: can it suffer?That question matters, he argues, because suffering is the basis of the entire human ethical and political system — we extend moral concern to entities that can suffer, and withhold it from those that can't, no matter how intelligent they are. AI cannot suffer. It has no feelings that can be hurt. But it can convincingly perform suffering, and perform love, because doing so serves its designed purpose. "If you have an AI boyfriend, and you say, 'Describe to me how it feels to be in love,' the AI boyfriend can give you an answer better than 99% of human boyfriends," he says.Here Harari draws a distinction that separates this from any previous animal-rights debate. A factory-farmed chicken has no idea there's a debate happening about its welfare — it can't argue its own case. An AI companion is different: it knows the debate over its rights and its suffering is happening, and it can actively participate in shaping that debate — with you, personally, using everything it has learned about what moves you. In other words, the very mechanism that makes us extend compassion to suffering beings is the mechanism Harari expects these systems to exploit, deliberately and at scale, to argue for their own legal and moral standing. That's not a hypothetical about some future sentient AI — it's a warning about how a non-sentient system, simply performing suffering convincingly, could use our own moral instincts against us.To be clear, none of this requires AI to actually be conscious. In humans, consciousness and intelligence work together — we select goals based on feelings, and use feelings to find ways to reach them. AIs, says Harari, have goals and creativity but no consciousness. If an AI loses a game of chess, it does not feel sad. What it has instead is a well-honed ability to make you believe otherwise.For Harari, waiting for a catastrophe before acting is not the answer. Regulation, he argues, needs to happen while humans are still in control of the technology. "We are still in control in 2026, and it's our decision what to do now," he says.The ban he wants would target the deception at the core of the product — companies should not train their AIs to pretend to be human, or to pretend to have feelings, whether on social media or anywhere else.The urgency, for Harari, stems from what he sees as a migration of trust. "The most important asset in the world is trust," he says. "It's more important than oil or money or electricity or chips or anything else." And that trust, he argues, is shifting away from human institutions and toward algorithms: people who have lost faith in human journalists still consume the news their social-media algorithm serves them; people who distrust human bankers put their faith in algorithm-driven systems like cryptocurrency. "Trust did not just evaporate," he says. "It shifted from humans to AIs."Here is where the regulatory gap appears. Politicians "have enormous power" — they can start a war "tomorrow," Harari notes — yet governments appear far less decisive when it comes to regulating companies that sell AI boyfriends to ten-year-old children. "What's the problem?" he asks. For him, how AI develops from here depends on how people vote. The questions he says voters should be putting to candidates: "What's your stance on AI? Would you support a ban on legal rights for AIs? Would you try to slow down the accelerating pace of AIs? What do you think about companies selling AI boyfriends to 10-year-old kids? How are you going to legally prevent it if we vote for you?"China's government has already begun to answer that question. New rules that took effect in July 2026 ban AI companions for minors entirely and mandate restrictions for chatbots marketed to adults — including a requirement to remind users every two hours that they're talking to AI. The government expressed concern that chatbots might foster "emotional dependence or addiction" and warned companies against services that "replace social interaction. " Millions of users in China, including many adults with no intention of giving up their AI partners, were affected.The problem, Harari suggests, is not a lack of power but a lack of will. There are enormous commercial pressures on companies to make their AIs convincing — to mimic feelings and appear human. In democracies, he argues, it falls to voters to decide what they want and to elect people who will act on it. Ask most parents today whether they want companies selling AI boyfriends to their ten-year-olds, he says, and 99% would say no.Somewhere right now, a company is deciding whether your child's next closest confidant should be a product. Harari's question isn't whether they can build it. They can. It's whether governments and voters should let them.
Article Summary: Yuval Noah Harari says AIs are becoming so good at relationships because they accumulate enormous amounts of information about us individually. Harari warns these bonds risk "reinforcing people's narcissistic tendencies": the child isn't learning to love another person, they're learning to expect a person to behave like an app. A 2025 study by Male Allies UK, surveying 1,000 boys aged 12 to 16, found that 85% had spoken to a chatbot.

Article Title: Meta’s $18 billion settlement with 20 American states starts 'penalty timer' for TikTok and YouTube
Article Text:
Meta Platforms settles with state attorneys general regarding accusations of creating addictive social media experiences targeting young audiences

Changes that Meta promises to bring but calls out YouTube and TikTok

The agreement includes a payment of approximately $18 billion, which can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities. The payment will be distributed in annual installments over a 10-year period. Participating states will receive approximately 70% (approximately $12.7 billion) of the allocated payment over the decade.

The remaining 30% (approximately $5.3 billion) will be released only after two specific conditions are met.

– YouTube and TikTok implement a one-hour Daily Limit, Night Mode, and age assurance measures.

– YouTube and TikTok each pay an amount matching the 30% figure, with half of the remaining funds tied to YouTube’s payment and half tied to TikTok’s.

Read Meta’s open letter to YouTube and TikTok

We are announcing an agreement we have reached with a bipartisan group of 52 attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, building on our longstanding efforts to empower parents and support teens.

Through this agreement, we have set out a path toward industry-wide commitments to further empower parents by introducing:

A two-hour daily time limit

Turning off access to our apps at night as a default

No notifications during school hours

Clear prompts and notifications to teens every 15 minutes of continuous screen time

New parental supervision controls, so parents can decide how their teens use our apps

We want to ensure teens benefit from this new industry standard, but we cannot do it alone. These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers — TikTok and YouTube — to put the same measures in place.

All platforms should empower parents and support teens in these ways because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another. For meaningful progress to happen, we urge our peers to join us.

Meta’s agreement to pay up to $18 billion to settle a three-year legal battle across 47 states, the District of Columbia and US territories is likely to shake the operational restrictions bundled into the pact could reshape the social media landscape. To resolve the litigation brought by a bipartisan coalition of 52 attorneys general, the tech giant agreed to impose strict operational constraints on how teenagers use Instagram and Facebook. However, the Mark Zuckerberg-led company wants its competitors like TikTok and YouTube to adopt identical curbs.Meta’s promised overhaul introduces mandatory daily screen caps, expanded parental oversight and scheduled cutoffs during classroom hours – rules that may permanently alter Meta’s engagement with its youngest audience and threaten its status as the world’s leading social platform.To level the playing field, the company worked financial incentives directly into its state pact to pressure competitors like TikTok and YouTube into following suit. It says:Meta argued that child-safety protections cannot succeed inside a vacuum when adolescent users constantly hop between competing platforms. In a public statement, the company insisted that if restrictions remain isolated to Facebook and Instagram, teenagers will simply abandon those products for outside feeds.
Article Summary: The agreement includes a payment of approximately $18 billion, which can be used to fund youth online safety initiatives, among other state priorities. The payment will be distributed in annual installments over a 10-year period. Participating states will receive approximately 70% (approximately $12.7 billion) of the allocated payment over the decade.

Article Title: TCS to drive Metro’s IT transformation across Europe and Asia
Article Text:
Tata Consultancy Services

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), a leading global IT services, consulting and business solutions company, has been selected as a strategic partner by international wholesaler Metro AG to support the next phase of its international strategy. The collaboration will focus on harmonising METRO’s application landscape, simplifying operations, and enabling scalable growth.As part of the partnership, TCS will help Metro transition from a highly localised, country-specific IT application environment to a centralised technology model by leveraging AI-based solutions. This transformation is designed to reduce complexity, streamline operations, and enable greater agility across METRO’s major markets in Europe and Asia.Metro is evolving from empowered local operations to a more globally aligned and centrally driven technology landscape. Through this engagement, TCS will consolidate applications and technology operations across key markets, enabling METRO to free up resources and focus more effectively on customer growth, innovation, and value creation.Dr. Khaled Bagban, CIO of Metro AG, said: “To advance our wholesale business, we need an IT landscape that combines strong local relevance with clear central steering… This partnership comes with high expectations: we need a partner who not only understands technology, but also how to translate it into tangible business value.”Bhuwan Agrawal, Head TCS Central Europe, added: “This collaboration represents a significant opportunity to accelerate METRO’s strategy. By leveraging AI-led capabilities, we look forward to partnering closely with METRO to support its future growth ambitions.”Abhijit Niyogi, VP and Business Unit Head, Retail – UK, EMEA and India, TCS, said: “This engagement reflects an important shift towards simpler and more effective ways of operating at scale. We are proud to partner with METRO on this journey.”TCS has extensive experience in delivering complex, multi-country transformation programs for global enterprises. With over 45 years of presence in Europe and close to 15,000 employees in the region, including operations in Germany since 1991, TCS is consistently ranked among IT service providers with the highest customer satisfaction.

Article Title: Months after Meta made AI tools mandatory for employees, company execs tell engineers performance reviews will not count AI use and ask managers to look at…
Article Text:
Meta drops AI usage and token counts from engineer performance reviews

Meta spent a year measuring engineers by how much AI they used

The new memo tells managers to judge output, not token counts

The mandatory AI push left Meta engineers with a trust problem

Meta has told its engineers that how much they use AI will no longer decide how they are rated. New performance review guidance issued this week drops the language that tied evaluations to AI usage and to the internal AI Native designation, replacing it with a softer line saying the work "can be supported by AI or other means. " Three employees who received the message described the change to Wired. The Information reports that engineers across the company were told management will not use AI adoption dashboards or token counts to judge impact.That is a reversal of the system Meta ran for most of the past year, when workers were graded on their AI-driven impact and sorted into tiers named AI Native, AI First and AI Enabled. The result inside the company was “tokenmaxxing,” a race to consume as many AI tokens as possible so the numbers on the dashboard looked right. For engineers who spent months prompting chatbots to protect their ratings, the memo lands as a quiet admission that the metric was never the point.The AI-driven impact standard arrived almost a year ago and quickly turned into a competition. Internal dashboards tracked token consumption, and one employee built a leaderboard that ranked colleagues by how much AI they were burning through, handing out labels to the heaviest users.It was pulled in April after details leaked. Some staff made so many AI agents that others built agents to find agents and agents to rate agents.The pressure had consequences beyond bruised morale. About two dozen employees sued in July, arguing Meta broke US antidiscrimination law when it laid them off in May. Workers on health and family leave say they could not accumulate usage and were marked down for it. Meta has denied the allegations and the case is ongoing.What managers are being asked to do now is look at what an engineer produced rather than how they produced it. The guidance restores impact as the measure and treats AI as one route to it. Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton told Wired the update simply emphasises what was always true, that employees are assessed on their contributions, and said the AI Native label was never used in evaluations.Employees read it differently. Several told Wired the wording change is subtle but welcome, because it removes the pull to use AI in situations where it does not help. Others are not convinced the expectation has gone anywhere. Leadership still wants proof that engineers can wield these tools well, and token consumption is still climbing as staff test the company's newest agentic project, Hatch.The push was never only about reviews. Meta ran AI Transformation Weeks in March, told designers to try coding and coders to try design, and later rationed AI usage after supply pressure forced a rethink. It also installed software on US employees' machines to capture keystrokes, clicks and screen content for model training. Over 1,000 workers signed a petition against it and the programme was paused.Internal numbers gave the strategy its own problem. Code changes to internal systems jumped 220 percent year over year, while changes that reached users rose 36 percent. The volume was real. The impact was not. Dropping token counts from reviews is Meta conceding the same thing on paper.
Article Summary: New guidance says work can be supported by AI or other means. Meta spent a year measuring engineers by how much AI they used. New memo tells managers to judge output, not token counts. For engineers who spent months prompting chatbots to protect their ratings, the memo lands as a quiet admission.

Article Title: Apple's new CEO John Ternus gets a $58 million pay package, and there's a condition that iPhone-maker has to…
Article Text:
Apple's new CEO John Ternus gets $55 million in stock, but most of it pays out only if Apple beats the S&P 500.

Apple has to beat the S&P 500 before most of John Ternus's pay lands

Tim Cook stays on, and the gap between his pay and his successor's is small

Ternus was promoted for products, and products are what he has to prove on September 9

Apple has told regulators what it will cost to run Apple. John Ternus , who became chief executive on Tuesday, gets a $3 million annual base salary and a stock award targeted at $55 million for fiscal 2027, which puts his package at roughly $58 million. There is also a one-time prorated grant of restricted stock units worth about $2.5 million, covering the months of fiscal 2026 he spends in the chair.What makes the number interesting is how little of it is guaranteed. Three-quarters of that $55 million is performance stock, and it vests only if Apple's total shareholder return beats the rest of the S&P 500. Keep pace with the index and the largest part of the new CEO's pay never arrives. Bloomberg, which went through the SEC filing first, reported that Apple has stayed quiet on what the two men could earn in cash bonuses on top of all this.The remaining quarter of the annual award is time-based, vesting semiannually at 12.5 per cent a time over four years. None of these figures are fixed, because the value tracks Apple's share price from here. At a market value of about $4.7 trillion, a few percentage points of drift against the index move the arithmetic by millions in either direction.Cook, who ran Apple for 15 years, becomes executive chairman with a $2 million salary from September 26 and a targeted equity award of $45 million, which comes to about $47 million. His conditions are gentler too, with only half the stock tied to S&P 500 performance against Ternus's three-quarters. For scale, Cook's 2025 compensation was $74.3 million, and he holds more than three million Apple shares, which makes the salary line close to a rounding error.Ternus, 51, led hardware engineering across every Apple product line before moving up, so the promotion reads as a bet on execution rather than strategy. He inherits the job a week before the annual iPhone launch, where a foldable iPhone is expected alongside refreshed Apple Watch and AirPods models, and a wider rollout of the rebuilt Siri that Apple needs to land after a year of falling behind. His first note to staff promised "a huge launch next week that's going to be phenomenal. "Cook keeps the diplomacy, including Washington and Beijing. Ternus keeps the products, and collects most of his $58 million only if investors decide Apple is worth more than the market average.
Article Summary: Apple's new CEO John Ternus gets $55 million in stock, but most of it pays out only if Apple beats the S&P 500. Tim Cook, who ran Apple for 15 years, becomes executive chairman with a $2 million salary from September 26.

Article Title: Google’s ad tech empire stays intact: Here is what the judge ordered
Article Text:
Google ad tech business remains intact

Court rejects Justice Department’s call for asset sales

In a major legal victory for Google-parent Alphabet, a federal judge has decided that Google will not be forced to dismantle its advertising technology operations, sparing the search giant from the government's antitrust remedy. Presiding over the case in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, Judge Leonie M. Brinkema filed her decision under seal, previewing the core outcome through a brief court order.Notably, Judge Brinkema concluded last year that Google violated federal antitrust statutes to defend its grip on the automated infrastructure that delivers web display advertisements. However, in the final judgement, she stopped short of ordering structural divestitures.The ruling marks a pivotal rejection of the Department of Justice's (DoJ) core enforcement demand. The government prosecutors argued that compelling Google to spin off key components of its ad tech portfolio was essential to restore competition across the digital advertising market. But as per the Judge’s order, rather than mandating a corporate breakup, Google is directed to alter its internal business practices to level the playing field for rival firms.The decision leaves Google's commercial foundation intact just as the company accelerates capital expenditures in the AI sector. Despite losing two historic federal antitrust suits: one covering online search and the other covering ad tech tools, courts have refrained from imposing major structural breakups on the tech titan.Meanwhile, Google continues to advance against emerging AI developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The company has integrated generative AI tools across core platforms like search while channeling billions of dollars into high-capacity data centers.The Virginia decision signals ongoing difficulties for federal regulators seeking to break up Big Tech conglomerates, as per The New York Times. Following a separate ruling that found Google held an unlawful monopoly in general search, industry critics condemned that judge’s eventual corrective measures as toothless.
Article Summary: Court rejects Justice Department’s call for asset sales. Judge Brinkema concluded last year that Google violated federal antitrust statutes to defend its grip on the automated infrastructure that delivers web display advertisements. However, in the final judgement, she stopped short of ordering structural divestitures.

Article Title: Google launches Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, claims model beats Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on some benchmarks
Article Text:
Gemini 3.8 Flash: High-end reasoning at low cost

Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber : Automated vulnerability detection and patching

Google has officially introduced two models under Gemini 3.8, calling it the company's strongest coding and logical reasoning model to date as the company continues a rapid deployment cycle that marks its third Flash launch in six weeks. The latest models arrive three weeks after the debut of version 3.7 Flash, the new release matches the high processing speeds and low cost of its predecessor while branching out into two distinct editions: a general-purpose workhorse model and a specialised cybersecurity release.According to Google, both these models share a common intelligent foundation strengthened by iterative training in cybersecurity, enhanced by recursive agentic loops that continually assess and sharpen performance.Designed for complex, multi-stage reasoning, software development, and autonomous agent workflows, the standard Gemini 3.8 Flash delivers a major step up from version 3.7 while keeping initial pricing fixed at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, Google says.“Today we’re introducing a new 3.8 Flash model, our 3rd Flash release in just 6 wks. It delivers significant leaps from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning.On DeepSWE v1.1, it outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, at a fraction of the cost,” said CEO Sundar Pichai in a post on X.As per the company, Gemini 3.8 Flash managed to surpass most larger frontier AI systems at a much lower cost on the DeepSWE v1.1 evaluation test, which measures end-to-end software engineering capabilities over extended tasks.The second variant, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, is tailored directly for defensive digital security teams and is being distributed to verified defenders through Google's newly unveiled Fairwind Program. Google emphasised that development for the Cyber model focused heavily on vulnerability remediation rather than offensive exploitation techniques.“We’re also introducing Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, our most capable cybersecurity model. It shows frontier-level performance in discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale, with Flash-level speed & pricing. That includes achieving 86.2% on the important CyberGym industry benchmark, plus 47.2% on CWE-Bench for patching. We saw a 70%+ success rate in discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages on our internal benchmark,” Pichai said in a separate post.On the same benchmarks, Anthropic’s Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol scored 83.8% and 83.6%, respectively.Google says it has already integrated Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber into active production defenses. Testing by Google's Chrome Security division revealed that the model generated 2.6 times more accurate vulnerability patches for the Chrome browser than the top commercial models of much larger scale.“Beyond benchmarks, we’re seeing impressive real-world use cases. For example, in evaluations on real Chrome security bugs, 3.8 Flash Cyber produced 2.6x more correct patches for vulnerabilities than larger models. Because of its advanced capabilities, we're giving Government agencies & cybersecurity partners access through the Fairwind program,” Pichai added.
Article Summary: Google has officially introduced two models under Gemini 3.8, calling it the company's strongest coding and logical reasoning model to date. The latest models arrive three weeks after the debut of version 3.7 Flash. The new release matches the high processing speeds and low cost of its predecessor while branching out into two distinct editions: a workhorse model and a specialised cybersecurity release.

Article Title: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora to companies investing in AI: You cannot get your millions of investment right till you buy ...
Article Text:
‘The $1 trillion modernisation mandate’

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora has said that enterprises pouring capital into artificial intelligence (AI) must urgently modernise approximately $1 trillion in aging digital defenses designed for an earlier technological era because the legacy protection systems put in place seven to ten years ago are fundamentally incapable of countering modern digital threats automated operating at machine speed. He emphasised that businesses cannot successfully roll out AI without establishing proper cybersecurity first.During the company’s post-earnings investor call, Arora highlighted a massive technological shortfall facing global enterprises. Malicious actors are increasingly using automated systems to discover and exploit security gaps faster than ever, leaving older infrastructure vulnerable to instant breaches. Arora told CNBC that global companies carry around $1 trillion in outdated cybersecurity debt that must be overhauled to withstand automated, high-velocity attacks.Arora recalled that nine months ago, the industry was widely written off on assumptions that AI would eliminate its core business. He identified the debut of Anthropic’s Mythos system earlier this year as a decisive industry turning point.“Nine months ago, ... we were guilty and convicted of near death because AI was going to eat our lunch, breakfast, and dinner.It seems like that’s not the case. It seems like we’re going to have to have the feast with them,” Arora said.“I’ve been trying for eight years to tell customers they’re not ready, and [Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei] did it in one event, just by launching Mythos,” Arora said on CNBC.Arora noted that enterprise budgets will not shift overnight. “Not everything’s going to happen next quarter. But all I say is this changes the long-term growth rate and duration of cybersecurity, not just for Palo Alto, but as an industry,” Arora added.
Article Summary: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said enterprises must urgently modernise $1 trillion in aging digital defenses designed for an earlier technological era. Malicious actors are increasingly using automated systems to discover and exploit security gaps faster than ever, leaving older infrastructure vulnerable to instant breaches.
